token-playground.name: Token Playground
token-playground.description: See how large language models tokenize text, assign next-token probabilities, and change sampling behavior with temperature.
token-playground.seoTitle: Token Playground — How LLM next-token prediction works | AhaFrame
token-playground.quick: LLMs generate text by repeatedly estimating probabilities for the next token, selecting one, appending it to the context, and repeating the process.
takeaways: Models read and write token units.
The chosen token becomes new context.

challenge.title: Choose decoding settings for structured output
challenge.body: Would you use the same temperature for creative copy and strict JSON? Explain the trade-off before opening the next lab.

guide.title: How does next-token prediction work?
guide.intro: A large language model generates text by estimating a probability distribution over possible next tokens, selecting a token using a decoding strategy, adding the selected token to the current context, and repeating the process.

sections.title: What is a token?
sections.body: A token is a text unit used by the model. It can be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, whitespace, or another fragment depending on the tokenizer.

sections.title: What does temperature change?
sections.body: Temperature changes the shape of the sampling distribution. Lower values concentrate probability around top candidates; higher values give lower-ranked candidates more chance to appear.

sections.title: Why does this matter in engineering?
sections.body: Decoding choices affect variability, deterministic behavior, structured-output reliability, and how an application balances creativity with control.

faq.q: Does an LLM choose a whole sentence at once?
faq.a: No. Autoregressive language models generate incrementally, token by token.

faq.q: Is a token always a word?
faq.a: No. Token boundaries depend on the tokenizer and can split words or include punctuation.
No. It changes sampling behavior, not the model weights or underlying knowledge.

faq.q: Are the probabilities in this lab from a live model?
faq.a: No. This MVP uses deterministic educational values so the learning experience stays stable.

guide.note: Interactive values are illustrative; conceptual explanations are the durable learning content.

context-window.name: Context Window Lab
context-window.description: Visualize how an LLM context window fills up and compare summarization, RAG, memory, and truncation strategies.
context-window.seoTitle: Context Window Lab — Context engineering visual lab | AhaFrame
context-window.quick: A context window is the model’s finite working input budget; system instructions, conversation history, documents, and tool results all compete for that space.

labels.beforeRisk: Risk: little space remains for new turns.
labels.principle: Context engineering is trade-off management: keep the most useful information available while controlling cost, latency, and information loss.

strategyNotes.drop: 47,350 tokens removed; 56,100 tokens of headroom remain. Fast, but older turns are lost.
strategyNotes.summarize: 78,820 tokens condensed or removed; 87,570 tokens of headroom remain.
strategyNotes.rag: 94,450 tokens removed from active context; 103,200 tokens of headroom remain as documents move to on-demand retrieval.
strategyNotes.memory: 62,950 tokens removed from active context; 71,700 tokens of headroom remain as stable facts move to persistent memory.

takeaways: Inputs compete for a limited working budget.
They preserve less detail but free capacity.
External knowledge need not stay in context.
Persistent facts are not the same as active context.

challenge.title: Design a context strategy for a support agent
challenge.body: Decide what stays in the prompt, what becomes a summary, what goes to retrieval, and what belongs in persistent memory.

guide.title: What is an LLM context window?
guide.intro: A context window is the finite amount of input information a model can process for a generation step. System instructions, user and assistant messages, retrieved passages, tool outputs, and other supplied content all consume that working budget.

sections.title: What happens when context becomes too large?
sections.body: An application must decide what to remove, compress, retrieve later, or persist elsewhere. The correct choice depends on which information is important for the next model decision.

sections.title: How is RAG different from memory?
sections.body: RAG retrieves relevant external information when needed. Memory usually refers to information persisted across turns or sessions. Both can supply context, but neither is identical to the context window itself.

sections.title: Why is context engineering important?
sections.body: Good context design improves relevance and reliability while helping control token cost and latency. More context is not automatically better context.

faq.q: Is context the same as memory?
faq.a: No. Context is the current working input; memory is a persistence strategy that may later supply context.

faq.q: Does RAG increase the context window size?
faq.a: No. RAG selects information to place inside the available context.

faq.q: Should I always summarize old messages?
faq.a: No. Summarization trades detail for compactness and can remove information that later becomes important.

faq.q: Are the token limits shown here model-specific?
faq.a: The 200,000-token value is an educational example, not a claim about every model.

guide.note: The lab uses a stable simulated token budget to make trade-offs observable.

agent-loop.name: Agent Loop Simulator
agent-loop.description: Step through an AI agent loop: understand the task, choose an action, call a tool, observe the result, recover from errors, and answer.
agent-loop.seoTitle: Agent Loop Simulator — How AI agents use tools and observations | AhaFrame
agent-loop.quick: An AI agent repeatedly decides what to do next, acts through tools, observes the result, and uses that observation to decide whether to continue, retry, or answer.
learn: How agent loops differ from chat
agent-loop.controlCopy: Use the simulator controls to advance one step at a time, reset state, or inject a failure.

labels.taskText: Find the weather in Tokyo and tell me if I need an umbrella.
labels.toolValue:
Tokyo · Light Rain · 18°C
Humidity 92% · Wind NE 12 km/h

The agent selects the weather tool.

Actions connect the model to external systems.
Tool output changes what the agent does next.
Retries and termination rules belong in the design.

challenge.title: Add a termination rule and fallback
challenge.body: Define when the agent should retry, when it should stop, and what it should tell the user when the weather tool stays unavailable.

guide.title: What is an AI agent loop?
guide.intro: An agent loop is an iterative control process in which a model or agent interprets the current state, chooses an action, receives an observation, and decides whether to continue or return a final answer.

sections.title: Why do agents use tools?
sections.body: Tools allow an agent to access information or perform actions that are not contained in the model itself, such as querying a database, calling an API, running code, or updating another system.

sections.title: What is an observation?
sections.body: An observation is the result returned from an action or tool. The agent uses that result as new evidence for the next decision.

sections.title: What makes an agent reliable?
sections.body: Production agents need explicit tool contracts, validation, retries, timeouts, authorization boundaries, observability, and termination conditions. The loop alone is not the reliability layer.

faq.a: No. A chatbot can answer directly without taking iterative actions through tools.

faq.q: Does an agent need hidden chain-of-thought?
faq.a: No. Agent control can be implemented through explicit state, tool calls, structured decisions, and observable transitions.
Because failures are normal in production; recovery behavior is part of the system design.

faq.q: Is ReAct the only agent pattern?
faq.a: No. Plan-and-execute, workflows, state machines, and other orchestration patterns are also common.
